notes:
1. Meaning of Right to Information

Right to Information is the legal right of every citizen to obtain information held by:

  • Public authorities.
  • Authorities exercising public functions.

It enables citizens to know:

  • How Government functions.
  • How decisions are taken.
  • How public money is spent.
  • How public programmes are implemented.
📌 Must-Memorise

RTI → Citizen's Legal Right to Access Information Held by Public Authorities

2. Governing Law

The Right to Information is governed by:

  • Right to Information Act, 2005.
📌 Must-Memorise

RTI Act → 2005

3. Nature of RTI

The Right to Information is a:

  • Statutory Right

under:

  • Right to Information Act, 2005.

At the same time, the Supreme Court has recognised the broader:

  • Right to Know

as flowing principally from:

  • Article 19(1)(a).
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

RTI under RTI Act → Statutory Right

Right to Know → Constitutional Principle under Article 19(1)(a)

4. Constitutional Foundation

The primary constitutional foundation is:

  • Article 19(1)(a) — Freedom of Speech and Expression.

Meaningful freedom of expression requires citizens to have access to relevant information.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 19(1)(a) → Right to Know

5. Objectives of RTI

The RTI Act seeks to:

  • Promote transparency.
  • Ensure accountability.
  • Empower citizens.
  • Reduce corruption.
  • Improve governance.
  • Increase public participation.
  • Strengthen democracy.
  • Balance disclosure with legitimate confidentiality.

6. What Is Information?

Information includes material in any form such as:

  • Records.
  • Documents.
  • Files.
  • Memos.
  • E-mails.
  • Opinions.
  • Advices.
  • Circulars.
  • Orders.
  • Reports.
  • Contracts.
  • Logbooks.
  • Samples.
  • Models.
  • Data.
  • Electronic records.

7. Information Relating to Private Bodies

RTI can also cover information concerning a private body where:

  • A public authority can access that information under an existing law.

8. Existing Information Only

The RTI Act gives access to:

  • Existing information.
  • Existing records.
  • Existing documents.

It does not require a public authority to:

  • Create new information.
  • Create an explanation not already on record.
  • Generate an opinion that does not already exist.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

RTI → Access to Existing Information

Not → Creation of New Information

9. Rights Included under RTI

Citizens may seek:

  • Inspection of records.
  • Inspection of documents.
  • Inspection of Government works.
  • Inspection of files.
  • Taking notes.
  • Taking extracts.
  • Certified copies.
  • Certified samples of materials.
  • Electronic information where available.

10. Culture of Official Secrecy

Before the RTI framework, public administration largely operated under:

  • Official secrecy.
  • Restricted access to Government records.

11. Official Secrets Act, 1923

The source identifies:

  • Official Secrets Act, 1923

as an important secrecy-related law protecting specified Government information.

📌 Must-Memorise

Official Secrets Act → 1923

12. Transparency Movement

Demand for greater access to Government information grew through:

  • Civil society movements.
  • Public-interest campaigns.
  • Judicial recognition of Right to Know.
  • Administrative reforms.

13. MKSS

The attachment identifies:

  • Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS)

as an important organisation in the transparency movement.

📌 Must-Memorise

MKSS → RTI/Transparency Movement

14. Freedom of Information Act, 2002

Before the RTI Act, Parliament enacted:

  • Freedom of Information Act, 2002.

The source states that:

  • It was not effectively operationalised.
  • It was later replaced by RTI Act, 2005.

15. Right to Information Act, 2005

The RTI Act created:

  • A practical statutory framework.
  • A legally enforceable mechanism.
  • Time-bound access to information.

16. Presidential Assent

RTI Act received Presidential assent on:

  • 15 June 2005.

17. Commencement

The substantive provisions came into force on:

  • 12 October 2005.
📌 Must-Memorise

15 June 2005 → Presidential Assent

12 October 2005 → Substantive Provisions in Force

18. Extent

The source states that the RTI Act now extends to:

  • Whole of India.

19. Meaning of Public Authority

A Public Authority includes a body or institution established:

  • By or under Constitution.
  • By Parliamentary law.
  • By State Legislature law.
  • By Government notification or order.

20. Government-Owned and Controlled Bodies

The definition also includes bodies:

  • Owned by Government.
  • Controlled by Government.
  • Substantially financed by Government.

21. NGOs

Certain non-government organisations may also come under RTI where they are:

  • Substantially financed directly or indirectly by Government funds.

22. Examples of Public Authorities

Examples include:

  • Ministries.
  • Government Departments.
  • Constitutional Bodies.
  • Statutory Bodies.
  • Municipal Corporations.
  • Panchayats.
  • Public Sector Undertakings.
  • Government Universities.
  • Government Schools.
  • Government Hospitals.
  • Government-owned Companies.

23. PIO

Every public authority must designate:

  • Public Information Officers.

PIOs are responsible for implementing RTI requests.

📌 Must-Memorise

PIO → Main Officer Processing RTI Application

24. Duties of PIO

PIO must:

  • Receive applications.
  • Assist applicants where necessary.
  • Identify relevant records.
  • Collect information.
  • Supply information.
  • Reject only on lawful grounds.
  • Give reasons for rejection.
  • Inform applicant about appeal rights.

25. APIO

Public authorities may designate:

  • Assistant Public Information Officers.

Their role includes:

  • Receiving applications.
  • Receiving appeals.
  • Forwarding them to appropriate authority.

26. APIO Additional Time

Where an application is submitted through an APIO:

  • Five additional days are added to the normal response period.
📌 Must-Memorise

Application through APIO → +5 Days

27. PIO vs APIO

PIO:

  • Processes application.
  • Supplies information.
  • Makes decision on disclosure.

APIO:

  • Receives.
  • Forwards.
  • Facilitates filing.

28. Section 4

Section 4 requires public authorities to proactively publish specified information.

This is called:

  • Suo Motu Disclosure.
  • Proactive Disclosure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Section 4 → Suo Motu Disclosure

29. Meaning of Suo Motu Disclosure

It means:

  • Information is published voluntarily by public authority.
  • Citizen need not file a separate RTI request for it.

30. Information to Be Proactively Published

Public authorities should disclose matters such as:

  • Organisation and functions.
  • Powers and duties.
  • Decision-making procedures.
  • Rules and regulations.
  • Budget.
  • Subsidies.
  • Beneficiaries.
  • Public procurement.
  • Contact details.
  • Details of PIOs.

31. Importance of Proactive Disclosure

Effective proactive disclosure:

  • Reduces RTI applications.
  • Improves transparency.
  • Improves public access.
  • Reduces unnecessary secrecy.

32. Who Can File an RTI Application?

The source states that:

  • Any citizen may submit an RTI application.

33. Mode of Application

Application may be submitted:

  • In writing.
  • Electronically where facilities exist.

34. Reasons Need Not Be Given

An applicant is not required to give:

  • Reasons for seeking information.
📌 Must-Memorise

RTI Applicant → No Reason Required

35. Language of Application

Application may be made in:

  • English.
  • Hindi.
  • Official language of the area.

36. Application Fee

A prescribed fee may be payable:

  • Subject to applicable RTI Rules.

37. BPL Applicants

Applicants belonging to:

  • Below Poverty Line category

are exempt from application fee subject to:

  • Applicable rules.
  • Required proof.

38. Assistance to Applicants

PIO should provide reasonable assistance where the applicant is:

  • Illiterate.
  • Unable to write.
  • Disabled.

39. Application to Wrong Public Authority

If the requested information is held by another public authority:

  • Application should be transferred to appropriate authority.

40. Time Limit for Transfer

Transfer should be made:

  • As soon as practicable.
  • In any case within 5 days.
📌 Must-Memorise

Transfer of RTI Application → Within 5 Days

41. Applicant Must Be Informed

The applicant must be:

  • Informed of the transfer.

42. Ordinary Time Limit

Information must ordinarily be supplied within:

  • 30 days.

Normal RTI Reply → 30 Days

43. Life or Liberty

Where information concerns:

  • Life.
  • Liberty.

it must be provided within:

  • 48 hours.
📌 Must-Memorise

Life or Liberty → 48 Hours

44. APIO Time Limit

Application through APIO:

  • Normal period + 5 additional days.

45. Third-Party Cases

Where third-party consultation is required:

  • Information should ordinarily be supplied within 40 days after prescribed procedure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third-Party Case → 40 Days

46. Time-Limit Memory

  • Ordinary → 30 days.
  • Life or Liberty → 48 hours.
  • APIO → +5 days.
  • Third Party → 40 days.

47. Grounds for Rejection

A request may be rejected only on grounds permitted under RTI Act such as:

  • Statutory exemption.
  • Information not held.
  • Disclosure prohibited by law.

48. Rejection Communication

PIO must communicate:

  • Reason for rejection.
  • Time limit for appeal.
  • Details of appellate authority.

49. When First Appeal Can Be Filed

First Appeal may arise from:

  • Rejection.
  • Incomplete information.
  • Delay.
  • Excessive fee.
  • Dissatisfaction with PIO decision.

50. First Appellate Authority

First Appeal lies before:

  • First Appellate Authority.

FAA is a senior officer within:

  • Same public authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Appeal → FAA → Same Public Authority

51. Time Limit for First Appeal

First Appeal should ordinarily be filed within:

  • 30 days

from relevant decision or expiry of response period, subject to Act.

52. Second Appeal

If dissatisfied after First Appeal:

  • Second Appeal may be filed.

53. Authority for Second Appeal

Second Appeal lies before:

  • Central Information Commission for Central matters.
  • State Information Commission for State matters.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Appeal → CIC / SIC

54. Time Limit for Second Appeal

Second Appeal should ordinarily be filed within:

  • 90 days.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Appeal → 30 Days

Second Appeal → 90 Days

55. Section 18 Complaint

A complaint may be filed before appropriate Information Commission under:

  • Section 18.

56. Situations for Complaint

Examples include:

  • Refusal to accept RTI application.
  • No PIO designated.
  • Other situations specified under Act.

57. Complaint vs Appeal

Complaint:

  • Separate statutory mechanism.
  • Filed under specified Section 18 circumstances.

Appeal:

  • Challenges decision, denial, delay or related RTI determination.

58. Meaning of CIC

The Central Information Commission is the highest statutory appellate authority for matters involving:

  • Central Public Authorities.

59. Establishment of CIC

CIC is established by:

  • Central Government

under:

  • Right to Information Act, 2005.

60. Composition of CIC

The attachment states that CIC consists of:

  • Chief Information Commissioner.
  • Information Commissioners as considered necessary by Central Government.

70. Qualifications of Information Commissioners

They should be persons of:

  • Eminence in public life.
  • Wide knowledge and experience.

  • Law.

  • Social Service.
  • Management.
  • Journalism.

75. Resignation

  • President.

State Information Commissioners resign to:

  • Governor.

76. Removal

  • Removed by President under Act.

State Commissioners:

  • Removed by Governor under Act.

77. Supreme Court Inquiry

For specified cases involving:

  • Proved misbehaviour.
  • Incapacity

the attachment notes that Supreme Court inquiry may be required before removal under statutory framework.

78. Civil-Court-Like Powers

While deciding complaints and appeals, Information Commissions have powers similar to Civil Court regarding:

  • Summoning persons.
  • Enforcing attendance.
  • Examining witnesses on oath.
  • Requiring documents.
  • Receiving evidence.
  • Inspecting records.

79. Functions

Information Commissions:

  • Hear Second Appeals.
  • Decide complaints.
  • Ensure compliance.
  • Direct disclosure where permitted.
  • Promote transparency.
  • Monitor RTI implementation.
  • Prepare Annual Reports.
  • Recommend record-management improvements.

80. Annual Reports

Both CIC and SIC prepare:

  • Annual Reports

on implementation of RTI Act.

81. Report Contents

Reports may contain:

  • Number of applications.
  • Appeals.
  • Complaints.
  • Penalties.
  • Recommendations.
  • Performance of public authorities.

82. CIC Report

Central Government lays CIC Annual Report before:

  • Parliament.

83. SIC Report

State Government lays SIC Annual Report before:

  • State Legislature.

84. Penalty on PIO

Information Commission may impose penalty on:

  • Public Information Officer

for specified violations.

85. Grounds for Penalty

Examples include PIO:

  • Refusing to receive application.
  • Failing to provide information in time.
  • Malafidely denying information.
  • Knowingly giving incorrect information.
  • Providing misleading information.
  • Destroying requested information.
  • Obstructing access.

86. Rate of Penalty

Penalty:

  • ₹250 per day of delay.

87. Maximum Penalty

Maximum penalty:

  • ₹25,000.
📌 Must-Memorise

RTI Penalty → ₹250 per Day → Maximum ₹25,000

88. Opportunity of Being Heard

Penalty is imposed after giving concerned PIO:

  • Reasonable opportunity of being heard.

89. Disciplinary Action

Apart from monetary penalty, Information Commission may recommend:

  • Departmental disciplinary action

under applicable service rules.

90. Penalty vs Disciplinary Action

Penalty:

  • Monetary.
  • Imposed by Information Commission.
  • Maximum ₹25,000.

Disciplinary Action:

  • Service-related.
  • Taken under applicable service rules by competent authority.

91. Need for Exemptions

RTI promotes disclosure but recognises that some information requires protection for legitimate interests such as:

  • National security.
  • Privacy.
  • Confidentiality.
  • Effective investigation.

92. Section 8

The attachment identifies:

  • Section 8

as containing major statutory exemptions from disclosure.

📌 Must-Memorise

Section 8 → Major RTI Exemptions

93. Sovereignty and Integrity

Information may be exempt if disclosure prejudices:

  • Sovereignty and integrity of India.

94. Security and Strategic Interests

Exemption may cover information affecting:

  • Security of State.
  • Strategic interests.
  • Scientific interests.
  • Economic interests of State.

95. Foreign Relations

Information may be protected where disclosure harms:

  • Relations with foreign States.

96. Court-Prohibited Information

Information expressly forbidden from publication by:

  • Court

may be exempt.

97. Legislative Privileges

Information may be exempt where disclosure would violate:

  • Parliamentary privilege.
  • State Legislative privilege.

98. Commercial Confidence

Exemption may apply to:

  • Commercial confidence.
  • Trade secrets.
  • Intellectual property

where statutory conditions are satisfied.

99. Fiduciary Information

Information held in:

  • Fiduciary relationship

may be protected subject to provisions of RTI Act.

100. Foreign Government Information

Information received in confidence from:

  • Foreign Government

may be exempt.

101. Safety of Individuals

Information may be withheld where disclosure would:

  • Endanger life.
  • Endanger physical safety.
  • Reveal confidential source under protected circumstances.

102. Investigation

Information may be exempt where disclosure would:

  • Impede ongoing investigation.

103. Cabinet Papers

Cabinet papers may be protected:

  • Subject to conditions specified in RTI Act.

104. Personal Information

Personal information may be protected where disclosure would cause:

  • Unwarranted invasion of privacy

unless:

  • Larger Public Interest justifies disclosure.
  • Disclosure is otherwise permitted by law.

105. Public Interest Override

Even where an exemption applies, disclosure may sometimes be justified by:

  • Larger Public Interest

subject to limitations in RTI Act.

📌 Must-Memorise

RTI Exemption + Strong Larger Public Interest → Disclosure May Be Permitted

106. Section 11

Third-party information is dealt with through consultation procedure under:

  • Section 11.
📌 Must-Memorise

Section 11 → Third-Party Information

107. Meaning of Third Party

Where requested information concerns another person or entity:

  • PIO follows prescribed third-party consultation procedure where applicable.

Transparency means:

  • Openness in Government functioning.

RTI allows citizens to examine:

  • Decisions.
  • Procedures.
  • Expenditure.
  • Policy implementation.
  • Public resources.

Accountability means:

RTI enables citizens to:

  • Examine official records.
  • Monitor implementation.

RTI supports:

  • Responsible administration.
  • Citizen participation.
  • Administrative efficiency.
  • Better service delivery.
  • Public confidence.

An informed citizenry can:

  • Participate in governance.
  • Make informed political choices.
  • Monitor Government.
  • Exercise democratic rights effectively.

112. RTI and Anti-Corruption

RTI can help citizens:

  • Detect misuse of public funds.
  • Examine contracts.
  • Verify welfare schemes.
  • Monitor recruitment.
  • Identify irregularities.
  • Improve financial accountability.

113. RTI and Citizen Participation

Citizens may use information to:

  • Monitor public projects.
  • Participate in discussion.
  • Examine expenditure.
  • Hold public authorities accountable.

114. RTI and Administrative Efficiency

RTI encourages authorities to:

  • Maintain records properly.
  • Improve documentation.

115. RTI and E-Governance

Technology strengthens RTI through:

  • Online RTI portals.
  • Electronic filing.

  • Electronic disclosure.
  • Digitisation.

116. Delay in Providing Information

Delays may arise from:

  • Heavy workload.
  • Poor record management.
  • Administrative delay.
  • Staff shortages.

117. Poor Record Management

Weak record systems may cause:

  • Missing records.

118. Low Public Awareness

Citizens may be unaware of:

  • RTI rights.

119. Misuse of RTI

The source notes that some applications may be:

  • Frivolous.

120. Privacy Challenge

Authorities must balance:

  • Right to Information.
  • Right to Privacy.

121. Transparency vs Confidentiality

Transparency:

  • General principle favouring disclosure.

Confidentiality:

  • Applies to information protected by statutory exemptions.

122. Capacity Constraints

Effective RTI requires:

  • Adequate staff.
  • Proper training.
  • Digital infrastructure.
  • Record management.
  • Administrative support.

123. Measures for Better Implementation

The source suggests:

  • Better record management.
  • Digitisation.
  • Stronger proactive disclosure.
  • Public awareness.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is RTI? → Legal right of citizens to obtain information held by public authorities.

Which Act governs RTI? → Right to Information Act, 2005.

What is the nature of RTI under the Act? → Statutory Right.

Which Fundamental Right provides constitutional foundation for Right to Know? → Article 19(1)(a).

What does Article 19(1)(a) guarantee? → Freedom of Speech and Expression.

Which law represented the older official-secrecy framework? → Official Secrets Act, 1923.

Which organisation is identified with India's grassroots RTI movement? → Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan.

What was enacted before RTI Act? → Freedom of Information Act, 2002.

Was it effectively operationalised according to the attachment? → No.

What replaced it? → RTI Act, 2005.

When did RTI Act receive Presidential assent? → 15 June 2005.

When did its substantive provisions come into force? → 12 October 2005.

What is “information” under RTI broadly? → Records, documents, files, e-mails, opinions, advices, circulars, orders, reports, contracts, data and electronic records.

Can information relating to a private body be obtained? → Yes, where a public authority can access it under law.

Does RTI require creation of new information? → No.

Does it require a public authority to invent an explanation not on record? → No.

Can citizens inspect Government works? → Yes.

Can citizens obtain certified copies? → Yes.

Can citizens obtain certified samples of materials? → Yes.

What is a Public Authority? → An authority/body established by Constitution, law or Government order and bodies owned, controlled or substantially financed by Government.

Can substantially Government-financed NGOs come under RTI? → Yes, according to the attachment.

Who is PIO? → Public Information Officer.

What is the main role of PIO? → Process requests and supply information.

Who is APIO? → Assistant Public Information Officer.

What is its role? → Receive and forward RTI applications and appeals.

How many additional days apply when application is filed through APIO? → Five.

Which Section requires proactive disclosure? → Section 4.

What is another name for proactive disclosure? → Suo Motu Disclosure.

Does citizen need to file an application for suo motu information? → No.

Can RTI application be electronic? → Yes, where facility exists.

Does applicant need to give reason for seeking information? → No.

Which languages can be used according to the attachment? → English, Hindi or official language of the area.

Who gets application-fee exemption subject to rules? → BPL applicants.

If information is with another public authority, within how many days should the application be transferred? → Five days.

What is ordinary RTI response time? → 30 days.

What is the time limit for Life or Liberty information? → 48 hours.

What is the third-party time limit stated in the attachment? → Ordinarily 40 days.

What must PIO provide when rejecting a request? → Reasons, appeal time limit and appellate authority details.

Where is First Appeal filed? → First Appellate Authority within the same public authority.

What is ordinary First Appeal period? → 30 days.

Where is Second Appeal filed? → CIC or SIC as applicable.

What is ordinary Second Appeal period? → 90 days.

Which Section deals with RTI complaints? → Section 18.

What is CIC? → Central Information Commission.

Which authorities fall under CIC? → Central Public Authorities.

Who establishes CIC? → Central Government.

Who appoints Chief Information Commissioner and Central Information Commissioners? → President.

Who are members of CIC appointment recommendation committee? → Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by Prime Minister.

Who chairs it? → Prime Minister.

What is SIC? → State Information Commission.

Which authorities fall under SIC? → State Public Authorities.

Who establishes SIC? → State Government.

Who appoints State Chief Information Commissioner and State Information Commissioners? → Governor.

Who are members of SIC recommendation committee? → Chief Minister, Leader of Opposition in Legislative Assembly and a State Cabinet Minister nominated by Chief Minister.

Who chairs it? → Chief Minister.

What qualifications are expected of Information Commissioners? → Eminence in public life and wide experience in fields such as law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media, administration and governance.

Can an Information Commissioner be a sitting MP or MLA? → No, according to the attachment.

Which Amendment changed tenure and service-condition framework? → RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019.

Does the Act still prescribe a fixed five-year tenure according to the attachment? → No.

Who prescribes term and service conditions after 2019? → Central Government through rules.

To whom does Central Chief Information Commissioner resign? → President.

To whom does State Chief Information Commissioner resign? → Governor.

What powers do Information Commissions have during appeals and complaints? → Civil-Court-like powers for summons, attendance, witnesses, documents, evidence and records.

Can Information Commission direct disclosure? → Yes, where legally permissible.

Who prepares Annual Reports? → CIC and SIC.

Where is CIC report laid? → Parliament through Central Government.

Where is SIC report laid? → State Legislature through State Government.

Who can be penalised under RTI Act for specified failures? → PIO.

What is penalty rate? → ₹250 per day.

What is maximum penalty? → ₹25,000.

Can disciplinary action also be recommended? → Yes.

Which Section contains major exemptions? → Section 8.

Give major exemption categories. → Sovereignty, security, foreign relations, court-prohibited information, legislative privilege, commercial confidence, fiduciary information, safety, investigations, Cabinet papers and protected personal information.

What is Larger Public Interest? → A public-interest consideration that may justify disclosure in specified circumstances despite an exemption.

Which Section deals with Third Party information? → Section 11.

What is the basic difference between transparency and accountability? → Transparency means openness; accountability means answerability.

How does RTI reduce corruption? → By allowing scrutiny of expenditure, contracts, recruitment, welfare schemes and Government records.

How does RTI support Good Governance? → By promoting openness, efficiency, responsibility and citizen participation.

What is the main challenge relating to privacy? → Balancing Right to Information with Right to Privacy.

Which case is called the foundation of Right to Know in the attachment? → State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, 1975.

Which case promoted Open Government? → S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981.

Which 1995 case recognised Right to Receive Information? → Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal.

Which case established voters' Right to Know candidate details? → PUCL v. Union of India, 2003.

Which case held evaluated answer sheets are information under RTI? → CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay, 2011.

Which case dealt with privacy of personal service records? → Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. CIC, 2013.

Which case emphasised financial transparency involving RBI? → RBI v. Jayantilal N. Mistry, 2015.

Which case recognised Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right? → K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017.

Which 2019 case held the office of Chief Justice of India is a Public Authority under RTI Act? → CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal.

What is the easiest RTI memory line? → Article 19(1)(a) gives the constitutional Right to Know; RTI Act, 2005 gives the statutory mechanism; Section 4 requires proactive disclosure; Section 8 provides exemptions; Section 11 deals with third-party information; CIC/SIC enforce the appellate system.
